documents.title: Mission and Theory of Change
documents.content:
# Tidewater Arts & Heritage Center — Mission and Theory of Change

Tidewater Arts & Heritage Center, Inc. is a 501(c)(3) public charity founded in 2011 and based in Charleston, South Carolina. Our work reaches Charleston, Berkeley and Colleton counties, including Johns, James, Wadmalaw and Edisto islands.

## Mission
Tidewater Arts & Heritage Center preserves, teaches and celebrates the living culture of the Gullah Geechee people of the South Carolina Lowcountry, so that the knowledge of elders passes to the next generation in their own words and hands.

## Theory of change
If elders' stories are recorded and kept in the community's care, and young people learn traditional arts directly from master artists, then Gullah Geechee knowledge, language and craft will be carried forward by the next generation. If the wider public experiences this culture first-hand at a free festival, then support for preserving Lowcountry heritage communities will grow.

## Our commitments
Every recording is made and shared only with the consent of the elder and their family. Master artists are paid for their teaching.

documents.title: Programme Descriptions
documents.content:
# Programme Descriptions

## Elders' Voices Oral History Archive
Trained interviewers record conversations with Gullah Geechee elders, in Gullah Geechee and English, in elders' homes and at the Center. Recordings are transcribed and shared through a free online archive with family consent. 46 new interviews were recorded in 2025-26, bringing the archive to 318 interviews.

## Youth Arts Apprenticeships
A 30-week after-school and Saturday apprenticeship for young people aged 13-18. Apprentices learn sweetgrass basket-making, music (spirituals, ring shout and drumming) or mural painting from 7 paid master artists, at the Center and 3 partner high schools. 84 apprentices enrolled in 2025-26.

## Tidewater Heritage Festival
A free two-day festival every May at Marsh Point Park in North Charleston, with Gullah Geechee food, music, crafts and storytelling. 11,500 people attended in May 2026.

## Plans
- Restore the 1898 Hollins Street Schoolhouse on Johns Island, acquired in 2022, as a permanent home for the archive and apprenticeship studios. Restoration is estimated at $1.4 million; $610,000 has been raised.

documents.title: 2025-26 Impact Report
documents.content:
# 2025-26 Impact Report

## Who we serve
- About 11,800 people took part in our programmes in 2025-26.
- 84 youth apprentices: 92% identify as Black or African American, and 71% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch.
- 46 elders recorded this year; narrators have an average age of 81, and 68% are aged 75 or older.

## Outcomes
- 75 of 84 apprentices (89%) completed the 30-week apprenticeship.
- Average master-artist portfolio scores rose from 1.8 to 3.9 on a 5-point scale between week 1 and week 30.
- 87% of apprentices said they feel more connected to their family's heritage.
- Apprentices created 4 public murals in Charleston and North Charleston.
- The Elders' Voices archive grew to 318 interviews and was streamed 14,200 times.
- 11,500 people attended the 2026 festival, where 62 Gullah Geechee artisans and vendors earned an estimated $148,000.

## In their words
"My grandmother sewed baskets on Highway 17 her whole life. Now I sew next to her, and people stop to watch me." — 16-year-old apprentice, Mount Pleasant

documents.title: FY2026 Budget Summary
documents.content:
# FY2026 Budget Summary

Annual operating budget (FY2026, year ending June 30, 2026): $920,000.

## Expenses
- Youth Arts Apprenticeships (master-artist fees, materials, transport): $268,000
- Elders' Voices Oral History Archive (interviewers, transcription, digital storage): $186,000
- Tidewater Heritage Festival (staging, security, artisan stipends): $142,000
- Facilities and building upkeep: $74,000
- Administration and finance: $138,000
- Fundraising: $112,000
- Total: $920,000

## Revenue mix
- Foundations: 42%
- Individual donors: 21%
- Government (humanities and arts council subgrants): 14%
- Corporate gifts: 11%
- Festival sponsorships and vendor fees: 8%
- Earned income (workshops): 4%

## Unit costs
- About $3,190 per youth apprentice per year.
- About $4,040 per new elder interview, including transcription and archiving.

## Capital (separate from operating budget)
Hollins Street Schoolhouse restoration: $1.4 million estimated; $610,000 raised to date.

documents.title: Governance and Capacity
documents.content:
# Governance and Capacity

- Board of 11 directors; meets every other month. Three directors are Gullah Geechee culture bearers, and one is a licensed historic preservation architect.
- An Elders' Advisory Council of 8 community elders reviews every archive release and festival programme.
- Most recent audit: FY2025 independent audit completed, clean opinion.
- Staff: 9 full-time, 5 part-time; about 160 festival volunteers and 22 trained oral history volunteers.

## Key leaders
- Odessa Manigault-Brown, Executive Director (since 2017); spends about 25% of her time on funder relationships.
- Darnell Washington, Programme Director; oversees the apprenticeships, archive and festival.
- Celeste Rivers, Development & Grants Manager (full-time); leads all grant applications and reporting.

## Federal experience
We have managed federal funds only as a subrecipient, through a National Endowment for the Humanities pass-through subgrant from the Palmetto Humanities Council ($25,000, 2025-26). We have not held a federal grant directly.

## Policies
Youth safeguarding policy, oral history informed-consent and family-rights policy, conflict of interest policy, whistleblower policy and document retention policy.

documents.title: Organisation Overview
documents.content:
# Organisation Overview (approved language)

Tidewater Arts & Heritage Center keeps Gullah Geechee culture alive and growing in the South Carolina Lowcountry. Since 2011 we have recorded the stories of community elders, in their own words and with their families' consent, building an archive of 318 interviews. Each year young people aged 13-18 spend 30 weeks learning sweetgrass basket-making, music and mural painting from paid master artists; in 2025-26, 75 of 84 apprentices completed the programme. Every May our free Tidewater Heritage Festival brings 11,500 neighbours and visitors together with Gullah Geechee artisans, cooks and musicians. Heritage, we believe, belongs to everyone.

opportunities.raw_text:
Cooper River Cultural Trust — Living Traditions Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Trust invites proposals from nonprofits in South Carolina's coastal counties that keep traditional and folk arts alive by connecting master artists with young people. Priority goes to culture bearers teaching within their own communities, including Gullah Geechee, Catawba and other heritage traditions. Awards range from $25,000 to $75,000 for one year. Eligible applicants are 501(c)(3) organisations with at least three years of programme history in traditional arts. Funds may cover artist fees, materials, youth stipends and transport. The Trust does not fund capital or building costs or one-off performances. Applications are due by 5:00 p.m. Eastern on the deadline date and must include a project narrative, project budget, most recent audit or financial review and board list. No match is required.

Sea Island Heritage Foundation — Oral Traditions Preservation Fund (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Foundation supports community-led projects that record, preserve and share the oral traditions of Gullah Geechee communities from coastal North Carolina to northern Florida. We fund interviews with elders, transcription, digital storage and public access, with a strong preference for projects where communities keep control of their own stories. Awards range from $20,000 to $60,000 over up to two years. Applicants must be nonprofits working within the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor and must submit a consent and community-access plan. We do not fund commercial licensing of recordings or research led by outside academic institutions. Proposals are due at midnight on the published deadline. No match required.

questions.prompt: Describe your oral history project and the community it serves.
questions.answer: Our Elders' Voices Oral History Archive records conversations with Gullah Geechee elders, in Gullah Geechee and English, in their homes and at the Center. Trained interviewers carry out each interview, and recordings are transcribed and shared through a free online archive with family consent. In 2025-26 we recorded 46 new interviews, bringing the archive to 318 interviews, which were streamed 14,200 times. Our narrators have an average age of 81, and 68% are aged 75 or older. We work across Charleston, Berkeley and Colleton counties, including Johns, James, Wadmalaw and Edisto islands. Supported by 22 trained oral history volunteers, the project keeps the knowledge of elders in the community's care.

questions.prompt: How will you protect the rights and wishes of narrators and their families?
questions.answer: Every recording is made and shared only with the consent of the elder and their family, under our oral history informed-consent and family-rights policy. An Elders' Advisory Council of 8 community elders reviews every archive release before it is made public. We do not license or commercialise elders' recordings. Our board of 11 directors includes three Gullah Geechee culture bearers, so community voices guide decisions at every level. Recordings are shared through a free online archive, keeping the stories in the community's care.

Lowcountry Preservation Trust — Historic Places Capital Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Trust awards capital grants to restore and stabilise historically significant buildings in Charleston, Berkeley, Dorchester, Colleton and Beaufort counties. We give priority to sites connected to African American and Gullah Geechee history, including schoolhouses, praise houses and community halls. Awards range from $50,000 to $250,000, paid over up to three years. Applicants must own the building, which must be at least 75 years old and listed on, or formally determined eligible for, the National Register of Historic Places at the time of application. A 1:1 cash match is required, and at least half of the match must be committed in writing when you apply. Applications must include a historic structure report or architect's condition assessment and a public access plan. We do not fund programme or operating costs, new construction or additions. Full proposals are due by 5:00 p.m. Eastern on the deadline date, following a required pre-application call with Trust staff.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: September 1 – October 31, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: September 1 – October 31, 2026

**Grant:** Edisto Community Arts Fund, Youth Arts Learning Grants — $60,000 (September 1, 2026 – August 31, 2027)

## Delivered so far
- The 2026-27 Youth Arts Apprenticeships cohort began on September 8, 2026, at the Center and 3 partner high schools.
- 82 young people aged 13-18 enrolled; 78 (95%) were still active at the end of October.
- 7 paid master artists taught 116 after-school and Saturday sessions in sweetgrass basket-making, music (spirituals, ring shout and drumming) and mural painting.
- Apprentices completed 8 of the 30 weeks.

## Who is taking part
- 91% of apprentices identify as Black or African American, and 70% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch.
- 31 apprentices are new this year; 51 returned from the 2025-26 cohort.

## Early outcomes
- Week-1 master-artist portfolio scores averaged 1.7 on a 5-point scale; the next scoring is at week 15 in January 2027.
- All 82 apprentices completed the pre-programme cultural-identity survey.
- Mural apprentices have finished designs for the first of this year's public murals, planned for North Charleston.

## In their words
"I didn't know the ring shout had steps you have to learn. Now I can lead one." — 14-year-old apprentice, Johns Island

## Spending to date
$21,400 of the $60,000 grant has been spent: master-artist fees $15,600, materials $3,900 and transport $1,900.

program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: July 1 – October 15, 2026

**Grant:** Stono River Heritage Foundation, Community Memory Grants — $40,000 (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027)

## Delivered so far
- 17 new interviews with Gullah Geechee elders were recorded, in Gullah Geechee and English, in elders' homes and at the Center.
- The Elders' Voices archive now holds 335 interviews, up from 318 on June 30, 2026.
- 12 of the 17 new interviews have been transcribed; 9 have been released online after review by the Elders' Advisory Council.
- 6 of our 22 trained oral history volunteers conducted interviews, including 4 on Wadmalaw and Edisto islands.

## Narrators
- Narrators recorded this period have an average age of 80; 11 of the 17 are aged 75 or older.
- Every recording was made with the signed consent of the elder and their family.

## Access and use
- The archive was streamed 5,100 times between July 1 and October 15, 2026.
- 3 Charleston County teachers used archive recordings in their classrooms this fall.

## In their words
"Hearing Mama's voice tell the story of the praise house, our grandchildren will know it the way we did." — daughter of an elder narrator, James Island

## Spending to date
$16,300 of the $40,000 grant has been spent: interviewer stipends $9,800, transcription $4,700 and digital storage $1,800. Spending is on plan.
